analysis.one_liner: Lets the Agriculture Secretary force companies to recall contaminated meat and poultry instead of asking.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, so USDA still cannot order meat or poultry recalls.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the Department of Agriculture cannot force a company to recall meat or poultry that may be unsafe; it can only ask, and the company decides whether to comply. This bill would change that, requiring anyone in the supply chain who suspects a product is unsafe to tell USDA, and letting the Secretary order a company to stop shipping and recall the product, with USDA notifying consumers directly. The bill never moved: it was sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, received no cosponsors, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers of meat and poultry. Today, when E. coli, Salmonella, or other contamination is found, USDA can ask a company to recall but cannot compel it; recalls move only as fast as the company chooses, and notices to shoppers are often the company's own. The bill would give the government the power to order contaminated product pulled from stores immediately and to tell consumers directly, closing a gap that has repeatedly left unsafe meat on shelves and in freezers during outbreaks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers who buy meat and poultry

how_it_helps.text: The bill would let the Secretary of Agriculture order a company to stop distributing and recall meat or poultry found adulterated or misbranded when there is a reasonable probability that eating it threatens public health [S3].

It would require any business that handles meat or poultry and has reason to believe the product is unsafe to notify USDA immediately, creating an early-warning system that does not exist in current law [S3].
When USDA had to order a mandatory recall, the Secretary — not the company — would provide notice to consumers who may have bought the product [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors, distributors, and retailers. They would bear the cost of mandatory recalls — pulling product from stores, notifying handlers, and losing the sale value of adulterated or misbranded inventory — and would lose the discretion they have today to contest, delay, or limit a recall. Some of those costs would ultimately show up in meat prices, but the bill imposes no new fees or taxes on consumers.

drawbacks.text: The bill would expose every handler of meat and poultry — including small distributors, grocers, and restaurants — to a duty to notify USDA and to mandatory stop-distribution and recall orders, with compliance costs that fall hardest on small firms.

Mandatory orders issue on the Secretary's own determination of a 'reasonable probability' of a public health threat, and while a firm can seek a hearing to vacate an order, the removal happens first and the challenge comes after — a burden on companies that believe their product is safe.
The bill adds no new funding or inspection resources, so its effectiveness would depend entirely on USDA's capacity to detect violations and enforce orders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — a government backstop when a meat or poultry company will not pull contaminated product on its own — is real and targeted at outbreaks that have already sickened people. The costs are modest and ordinary: recall expenses for companies, which would pass through in prices only at the margin, and a small risk that over-broad orders could burden firms handling safe product, which the bill addresses by requiring a hearing before an order is lifted. On balance, a consumer-safety improvement with limited downside; the drawback is less in the design than in the fact that it was never enacted or even considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Tom Udall introduced the bill on July 28, 2009, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The action history ends there: the committee took no further action on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing all legislation not passed [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors and distributors, who keep a recall system that is voluntary and company-controlled; no consumer gained because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and poultry processors and distributors

for.name: Tom Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks, but attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Meat and poultry industry
against.what_they_did: The meatpacking industry has long opposed giving USDA mandatory recall authority over meat and poultry, defending the voluntary recall system.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a party split to show: it had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would subject processors to mandatory USDA recall and stop-distribution orders for the first time, replacing today's system in which all recalls are voluntary and the company decides how fast and how widely to pull product. It would also formalize a handler notification duty, adding compliance costs, but would operate through the existing USDA inspection framework rather than adding a new regulator.

industries.industry: Meat and poultry distributors, wholesalers, and retailers
industries.note: Anyone handling tainted product would be required to cease distribution immediately upon USDA notification, meaning inventory losses and disruption for grocers and distributors even when they did not cause the contamination. Consumers benefit from faster removal of unsafe product from shelves.
